preview: An detailed account of the interview experience and selection process for an internship at Hilti by Sumit Mhaske.
content:
HTSI Interview Experience
Sumit Mhaske
Third Year
Information Technology
Location: Pune
Stipend: 80,000 INR.
Timeline
Online Test
The test had 61 questions for 90 mins in total and was held on Mettl, we had to allow camera and microphone access.
Coding Section
Mr. Myers and the Exam -
A mathematics question paper has a certain number of questions and each question is assigned some random maximum marks. Mr. Myers wants to edit the marks assigned to the questions such that:
1. All questions in the paper should have distinct maximum marks.
2. The total marks of all the questions should be as low as possible.
Mr. Myers wants to achieve this by making minimal changes in the original format, assigning the question at least as much marks as it originally had. Find the minimum total marks that he can set the paper for.
Input Specification:
Input1: The number of questions in the paper
Input2: The array representing the original marks assigned to every question.
Output Specification:
The minimum total marks Mr. Myers can set the paper for.
Solution: We simply need to maintain an unordered_set to check if an element has already occurred and then run a for loop. If the element is not present in the set, insert it. If it is present, increment the element by 1, decrement i (because the for loop will increment it, and we’ll decrement it so that it remains at the same index to check if the incremented value is present in the set or not).
Aptitude Section
This section had a 30-minute timer. The questions were quite easy; you just needed to think quickly and solve them fast, as there were 30 questions to complete in 30 minutes. Some were mental ability questions, while others required math (probability and statistics). The math questions were a bit challenging, so it's better to solve the non-math questions first.
Computer Fundamentals
This section had questions based on -
DSA -6
OS -6
OOPs -7
CN -6
DBMS -5
I finished my online assessment with around 10 minutes remaining. I submitted the test quickly because sometimes, when people get the same scores, they might judge you based on the time taken to finish. I had already checked my answers, so I didn't need to double-check them. You should double-check if you haven't.
Around 27 students were shortlisted for interviews. We received the shortlist between 3-4 PM on the next day (1st August), and the interviews were scheduled for 9 AM on 2nd August. I had already started preparing for the interview because I was confident about the questions I solved. On the day of the online assessment itself, I informed my senior, who had been guiding me throughout my preparation, that I was confident about the test and expected to be shortlisted, with my interview scheduled for the day after tomorrow. She arranged a mock interview for me in the morning so she could give feedback on certain topics, allowing me to prepare accordingly that day.
Note: Always verify your resume and seek preparation guidance from your seniors.
INTERVIEWS (Offline)
Technical Round
We were seated in the TPO hall and introduced to the panelists who came to interview us, consisting of six people, one of whom was from HR. The technical rounds ran simultaneously, with one interviewer assigned to each candidate. We were called in batches of five, and those deemed capable were sent directly for the HR round after 15 minutes to an hour of technical interviews (so be prepared for the HR round as well). I was 16th or 17th in the serial order, and my turn came just after the lunch break, around 1:45 PM. Don't forget to ask those who go for the interview before you about the questions they were asked, as sometimes the questions get repeated.
Finally, I was called in and greeted warmly by the interviewer. Always greet the interviewer with a smile and be confident. He took my resume and asked if I knew how much I scored in my online assessment. I replied that we weren't informed about the marks (at this point, you might feel a bit anxious, but remember—never doubt yourself in an interview). He then asked me to introduce myself and share some background information. Always have a brief introduction ready, about 1 to 2 minutes long.
The flow should be:
1. Name
2. Branch
3. Technical stacks/domains you've worked on (I focused on web development)
4. Achievements (hackathon wins, competitive programming awards)
5. Positions in clubs/internship experience
6. Hobbies
After this, he introduced himself and mentioned that he would share more about his career at the end of the interview (which I asked about at the end, making a good impression by showing curiosity and attentiveness).
He went through my resume and started with technical questions. He began with, "So you do C++, right?" and then asked me about the differences between C++ and languages like C, COBOL, and Pascal. I told him that I had never worked with COBOL or Pascal but that I was familiar with C, and I explained the differences between C and C++ (always be honest with your answers, and don’t hesitate to mention things you haven't done—they won't focus on those areas).
He then expanded on my explanation and asked about inheritance, specifically whether we can inherit everything from a parent class (the answer is no—private members cannot be inherited), and asked me to explain it with code. Another question from OOP was to explain function and operator overloading, also with code examples.
He then asked about my projects and requested that I explain one of them. Always follow the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) pattern when explaining your projects.
He went on to ask what exactly I did in this project, how I did it, the flow of data, and how we implemented it (make sure to remember the libraries you used in your projects). He was interested in the concepts and didn’t ask for any code.
Note: Be clear about the objectives of your projects, what you did to achieve them, and the technical details involved.
After this, he moved on to data structures and algorithms (DSA). He gave me a sequence of numbers written on a paper and asked me to implement a stack and a queue, then push this sequence into both and predict the output sequence when we pop all the elements. After that, he asked me to consider this as a depth-first search (DFS) of a tree and construct the tree, telling me that 54 (which was somewhere in the middle of the sequence) is the root.
The trick here is that since the root isn’t at the start or end of the sequence, it can’t be a preorder or postorder traversal—it must be an inorder traversal. This means all the elements on the left of the root are part of the left subtree, and those on the right are part of the right subtree. I constructed the tree and explained that the left and right subtrees of the root can be arranged in multiple ways because we don’t have further information.
Then he asked me to consider this as a breadth-first search (BFS) and construct the tree again. I pointed out that this can't be BFS because, in BFS, the root is always at the start, representing the top level of the tree.
This experience highlights that it’s not always about your coding skills; sometimes, you’re presented with trick questions where you need to act smart and think rationally.
Then he moved on to operating systems (OS) and asked me what paging is. The follow-up question was whether I knew how the Windows setting for 'changing page size' works. He then asked about race conditions and how to prevent them. When I mentioned locks along with other techniques, he asked what the similar concept is in DBMS. He was referring to Two-Phase Locking (2PL), so I explained transactions, concurrency, and 2PL. He also asked about normalization.
He then drew a table on paper, and I knew it was time for SQL. He asked me to write a simple query to retrieve data based on certain conditions (essentially using the WHERE clause). However, the follow-up was tricky. He drew another table and asked me to retrieve some attributes that were from both the first and second tables. Now, if I had mentioned joins, I would have been wrong because there were no common attributes between the tables. I pointed out this observation, and he smiled before adding a ‘serial_no’ column to the second table to create a common attribute. He then explained his requirements and asked me to write the query. It required the use of a nested loop, and after some thinking, I figured out the answer.
He then presented a quiz: We have three jars with capacities of 12 liters, 8 liters, and 5 liters. None of the jars have any markings on the inside. You can fill, empty, or transfer water between the jars. The task is to measure exactly 6 liters of water, meaning you need to have exactly 6 liters in one of the jars by following the given steps.
He gave me ample time, and I used paper to draw the transitions. After around 10 or more transitions, I managed to get 6 liters in one jar. (Hint: In these types of questions, focus on what extra amount you need to reach the target, compared to the capacity of the jar that is just smaller than the target, and try to achieve that by leveraging the differences in the jar capacities). You can find similar puzzles on GeeksforGeeks (GFG).
He then asked me if I had any questions about the work or the company. It's important to always scroll through the company's website and gather information from seniors and other sources. Be sure to prepare your questions based on this research (always ask questions—it shows that you're genuinely interested in the company). Make sure to ask relevant questions and try to come up with something unique, rather than just the common questions you find on the internet.
We talked about this for a while, and he explained everything in great detail, as he seemed interested in me. I also reminded him that he mentioned earlier that he would tell me about his career path, and he shared it with me.
At the end, he said, "I liked you pretty much. Just wait outside, and we'll call you for the next round." That moment was awesome. After coming out, I realized my interview had lasted around 80 minutes, while others were there for about 40-45 minutes. I felt pretty confident after that.
HR Round
My HR round started about 10 minutes after my technical interview ended. The HR interviewer asked me if my name was Sumit and if Amey Sir had conducted my interview, to which I replied yes. She then asked me to introduce myself and explain how I ended up in Mumbai, noting that my resume mentioned I was from Sabhajinagar (formerly Aurangabad). After that, she asked if I had any questions for her.
The interaction seemed somewhat like a formality, as she wasn't asking me many questions and initially confirmed whether I was the candidate Amey Sir had interviewed.
It was clear to me that she had likely already received feedback and that this HR round might just be a formality.
I then went outside to the TPO hall and waited calmly with my friends for the results. Around 5:30 PM, the HR along with her team came to announce the results. When she called my name first, I was overwhelmed with joy. Trust me, the feeling of seeing all my hard work pay off was incredibly rewarding and surpassed any other experience.
4 other candidates were offered internships along with me.
Resources
1. For DSA, I used Striver's a2z sheet, some people also consider another popular option, DSA450. I made notes for each topic because DSA is a long journey and it's easy to forget what was covered earlier. Also maintain the habit of giving CP contests.
2. For OS and DBMS, I studied thoroughly during the 4th semester and made notes at that time. These notes, created using the Gate Smashers playlist for both subjects, proved to be quite helpful later. The day before the interview, I reviewed InterviewBit PDFs, which were in a question-and-answer format and are also quite useful. (PDFs for React, mongoDb, SQL, OOPS are also available on interviewBit). For SQL, there's also a website named MariaDB tutorial that is well-organized and explains SQL in an easy manner.
3. For OOPs, I started with the one-shot video of OOPs in C++ from Apna College but found it necessary to study further using GeeksforGeeks (GFG) articles. Remember to study pointers and other C++ concepts if you're working with C++. Also, be prepared for questions like the difference between C++, Java, and C.
4. For HR preparation, many suggest Indiabix. While it’s a useful resource, I recommend figuring out your own answers to commonly asked HR questions. Having a unique perspective and avoiding generic answers can make a big difference.
Sumit Mhaske
Hilti Intern
